Iniquitous

in-IK-wi-tus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Iniquitous is grossly unfair and morally wrong.

Historians now describe the colony's labor system as iniquitous, a deeply unjust arrangement that enriched a handful of officials while workers starved.

Worked Example

Critics called the new toll iniquitous, since it charged the same flat fee to a delivery truck and to a family driving to a funeral.

Iniquitous is reserved for arrangements or actions that are not just unfair in a minor way, but wicked and unjust at their core.

How Iniquitous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

unjust

unjust: not fair or right

wicked

wicked: morally wrong or evil

Antonyms

equitable

equitable: fair and unbiased

righteous

righteous: morally good and just

How Strong Is It? — unfair → iniquitous → iniquitous

unfair vs. iniquitous

unfair vs. iniquitous: A referee's unfair call can be forgiven after the game.

iniquitous vs. iniquitous

iniquitous vs. iniquitous: An iniquitous system that traps generations in poverty demands to be dismantled.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Iniquitous comes from Latin iniquus ("unjust"), itself built from in- ("not") + aequus ("equal, fair") -- but centuries of use fused those pieces into a single borrowed word that no longer splits cleanly in modern English.

Use the root in a new word: equinox

Use the root in a new word: equinox: The same deeper root, aequus ("equal"), survives in "equinox" -- the day when daylight and darkness are of equal length.
